extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method; scientists concerned with evaluation of evidence and testimony
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing testimony, alleged anomalies (miracles, new kinds, coincidences), and the reliability of observation within inductive reasoning. Focuses on how prior probabilities, alternative hypotheses, witness motives, and the distinction between perception and inference affect credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracle testimony and antecedent improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: No evidence can prove a miracle to anyone who did not previously believe the existence of a being or beings with supernatural power; the only antecedent improbability ascribed to the miracle is the improbability that any such cause existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A miracle considered merely as an extraordinary fact may be certified by senses or testimony, but nothing can ever prove that it is a miracle because there is always the alternative hypothesis of some unknown natural cause. Those who already believe in a supernatural being must weigh the supernatural hypothesis against the unknown-natural hypothesis and judge which is the more probable in the particular case. The conformity of the result to the supposed agent's character (i.e., the Deity's character) is an important element. Given the general uniformity of nature, there is a presumption against divine agency not operating through general laws; thus every miracle has antecedent improbability that requires extraordinary antecedent probability from special circumstances to outweigh it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbelief when fact conflicts with ascertained causal law
rubrics_metrics.description: An assertion that a cause has been defeated of an effect connected with it by a completely ascertained law of causation is to be disbelieved or not according to the probability that there existed an adequate counteracting cause in the particular instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To estimate this, use previous knowledge of the frequency or rarity of known counteracting causes and consider only whether such a cause existed at the time and place alleged (not the general existence in nature). Judge how likely it is that such a cause would have been present without manifesting other marks, and whether the hypothesis of false testimony conflicts with higher-order generalizations. Degree of conviction should follow the preponderance of these probabilities, at least until further sifting of the matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling assertions of new Kinds (conflict with uniformities of co-existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an alleged fact conflicts with uniformities of mere co-existence (properties of Kinds), the assertion is the existence of a new Kind; this is not inherently incredible and should be rejected only if the improbability that such a variety remained undiscovered is greater than that of error or mendacity in the witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credible persons reporting unexplored places are not generally disbelieved but regarded as requiring confirmation from subsequent observers. Reject only if alleged properties are at variance with known properties of a larger kind (i.e., some properties said disjoined from others which have always accompanied them). If the generalization to be violated is very special and limited, suspend judgment and await inquiry; if the generalization is comprehensive, an alleged exception cannot be admitted unless supported by evidence of a causative law established by still more complete induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary contradiction to very general laws is essentially impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities true of all things, or independent of varieties of Kinds (laws of number and extension, and the law of causation), are probably the only ones exceptions to which are absolutely and permanently incredible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions that contradict these very general laws are confined to the word 'impossibility' (total impossibility). Violations of special laws of causation should be described as impossible only 'in the circumstances of the case' unless some cause existed which did not exist in the particular case. In practice, cautious persons will deem only such contradictions absolutely incredible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of judgment for plausible anomalies pending confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an anomalous assertion neither contradicts universal/general laws nor the most comprehensive generalizations, and when circumstances are not so thoroughly explored, a cautious person should neither admit nor reject the testimony but await confirmation from other unconnected sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is appropriate provided the testimony presents, when well sifted, no suspicious circumstances. Example: the King of Siam should have waited for confirmation when told of ice. Ignorant persons, by contrast, tend toward unreasonable credulity or contemptuous incredulity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize testimony for causes of untrustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: In many recorded instances where numerous reputable witnesses testified to things later found untrue, there are usually circumstances (fallacious appearances, epidemic delusion, strong interests like religious zeal, party feeling, vanity, passion for marvelous) that render the testimony untrustworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keen observers who sift the matter will often find means to account for impressions on senses/minds (optical delusions, contagious popular feeling, strong interest). Absence of such circumstances combined with non-contradiction to very general laws suggests waiting for confirmation rather than immediate acceptance or rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between improbability before the fact and improbability after it
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between the improbability of a mere guess being right (before the fact) and the improbability of an alleged fact being true (after being asserted). Many events improbable beforehand are not incredible once affirmed because not contrary to any approximate induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a die showing an ace is improbable beforehand but not disbelieved if a credible witness affirms it because some face must appear on a throw. Similarly, the fact that A.B. died yesterday may have had large odds against that specific day before it occurred, but once asserted, experience offers no ground to discredit testimony. Do not disbelieve events merely because chances were against them prior to their occurrence; consider whether the occurrence is still consistent with known inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate coincidences by assessing comparative probability of false assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidences (peculiar combinations of chances that resemble results of law) may be regarded as more improbable and thus thought to require stronger evidence, but whether they do depends on the comparative probability that the testimony would have been delivered if the fact were not true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider two sources of increased apparent improbability: (a) the rarity of the combination itself (e.g., ten sixes in succession), and (b) the heightened motive to assert wondrous occurrences (desire to astonish) which can increase mendacity. Laplace argued coincidences need more evidence because false assertions of rare events will concentrate on the rare event, but this presupposes a model of witness error that may be unjustified. For each coincidence, estimate from first principles the probability that given testimony would be made if the fact were false, accounting for witnesses who might be more careful when events seem extraordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model witness error carefully (Laplace critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing credibility of assertions about events with many alternatives versus binary alternatives, account for whether the witness's mistakes or interests are uniformly distributed across alternatives or concentrated, because this affects how often a particular false announcement will occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laplace's white/black ball vs numbered-ticket example shows that if a witness's false announcements are uniformly distributed among many distinct alternatives, a particular alternative will be falsely announced rarely; but if errors reduce to a binary choice, false announcements of the rare option may occur much more often. However, this reasoning requires that the witness's error model be representative; if a witness can avoid many errors when only one form is possible, Laplace's conclusion may fail. Thus, in assessing testimony, examine whether the structure of possible errors or motives makes falsehoods disproportionately likely for the extraordinary category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute effects to causes that make them likely
rubrics_metrics.description: When an observed regular series or peculiar result occurs, consider whether it is more naturally attributed to chance or to a cause which, if real, would be very likely to produce that result (e.g., design or unfairness in dice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A regular series is not less likely than an irregular one to be produced by chance, but it is much more likely to be produced by design or a constant cause. All else equal, attribute the effect to the cause that would most probably produce it. Use comparative probability of competing causal explanations (e.g., Laplace’s theorem: superior efficacy of a constant cause will quickly outweigh any antecedent probability against its existence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require direct observation (not inference) for relying on sensory reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole condition for relying on observation is that what is supposed to have been observed shall really have been observed; that it be an observation, not an inference. Much of what we call observation is a compound of sensation (direct perception) and inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that perception provides sensations (e.g., a sound, colored surface), whereas identification (a voice, a brother) is an inference from those sensations and prior habit. Errors of sense are usually erroneous inferences, not failures of sensation. Therefore, in judging testimony or observation, distinguish sensations (genuine) from inferential attributions (fallible) and be cautious where habitual inferences might be mistaken (optical deceptions, hallucinations, misidentification).

rubrics_metrics.name: For exceptions to comprehensive empirical generalizations, demand stronger induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the generalization which the alleged fact would violate is comprehensive and embraces a vast number and variety of observations, an alleged exception cannot be admitted unless supported by evidence of some law of causation proved by a still more complete induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat highly general empirical laws as approaching the certainty of ascertained laws of causation; to accept an exception, one must provide evidence not merely of isolated occurrences but of a causal law established by fuller induction. In practice, investigate whether unknown liabilities to counteraction or alternate origins of phenomena might account for apparent exceptions before overturning broad generalizations.
